title.en: Yemanjá's Bursting Womb: the Birth of the Orishas in Brazil
title.zh: 葉瑪雅裂腹誕神：巴西的奧利沙譜系

texts.period: Afro-Brazilian Nagô mythology; recorded late 19th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (published 1905/1906), ch. on the Nagô religion — the Yemanjá genealogy of the orishas

summary.en: From the marriage of Obatalá the Sky with Odudua the Earth were born Aganjú, the firm land, and Yemanjá, the waters. Yemanjá married her brother and bore Orungan, the Air, the heights, the space between earth and heaven; he conceived incestuous love for his mother, seized her while the father was away, and violated her. Mad with horror, Yemanjá wrenched herself from her son's arms and fled; he pursued her, and just as his hand was about to fall she died — and her body grew monstrously, and from her monstrous breasts two rivers gushed forth that met and made a lagoon; and from her enormous belly that burst came Dadá, Shangó, Ogún, Olokun, Olochá, Ogé, Ochun, Obá, Okó, Ochosi, Ajé-Chaluga, Chankpanná, the Sun, and the Moon.
summary.zh: 天父奧巴塔拉與地母奧杜杜瓦結合，生下堅土阿甘茹與眾水葉瑪雅。葉瑪雅嫁兄而生奧倫甘——空氣、高天、天地之間的空間。奧倫甘對生母生出亂倫之愛，趁父親外出擄母行惡；葉瑪雅瘋狂掙脫狂逃，追者將及，她倒地而死——屍身暴長，雙乳湧出二河匯成湖；巨腹迸裂之處，誕下植物之神達達、雷神香戈、鐵神奧貢、海神奧洛昆、湖神奧洛夏、尼日河神、奧順河神、歐巴河神、農神、獵神、醫神、天花神、太陽與月亮——十五位神祇。

sensitivity.note: Nina Rodrigues records the Yemanjá genealogy as told by Bahian Nagô heads — he notes it was relatively recent and contested by some Candomblé elders (Ifá and Elegbá have no place in it). Presented as a recorded variant of the diaspora pantheon-genealogy. Cross-ref: yoruba creation records.

passages.text: From the consortium of Obatalá, the Sky, with Odudua, the Earth, were born two children: Aganjú, the firm land, and Yemanjá, the waters. Marrying her brother Aganjú, Yemanjá gave birth to Orungan — the Air, the heights, the space between the earth and the sky.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues, Os Africanos no Brasil (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Orungan conceived an incestuous love for his mother, and taking advantage of the father's absence, seized her and violated her. Afflicted and delivered to violent despair, Yemanjá wrenched herself from the arms of her son, fled hallucinating, despising the infamous proposals for the continuation of the criminal love in secret. Orungan pursued her; but, close to laying hands on her, Yemanjá fell dead. Her body grows monstrously, and from her breasts, monstrous, two rivers are born which later unite, constituting a lagoon.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: From the enormous belly that bursts are born: Dadá, goddess-or orishá of the vegetables; Shangó, god of thunder; Ogún, god of iron and war; Olokun, god of the sea; Olochá, goddess of the lakes; Ogé, goddess of the river Niger; Ochun, goddess of the river Ochun; Obá, goddess of the river Obá; Okó, orishá of agriculture; Ochosi, god of the hunters; Oké, god of the mountains; Ajé-Chaluga, god of health; Chankpanná, god of smallpox; Orun, the sun; and Ochú, the moon. It is to be believed that this legend is relatively recent and little spread among the Nagôs: our negroes who direct the Yoruba cult, even those recently in Africa, are entirely ignorant of it, and some contest it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

texts.period: Afro-Brazilian Nagô mythology; recorded late 19th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (1906), ch. on the Nagô religion — the legend of Changó and the charm of Obatalá

summary.en: Changó, reigning in Ovó, was given by Obatalá a powerful charm which, swallowed, made him able to conquer all his enemies; he ate the greater part and gave the remainder to his wife Oyá to guard — who, in his absence, ate it too. The next day, in the council of ministers, when Changó's turn came to speak, he was transfigured, and flames came out of his mouth, dispersing the whole audience; the same happened to Oyá with her ladies. Certain now that he was an orishá, Changó stamped his foot on the ground, which opened and gave him passage with his three wives — only the end of the iron chain he carried in his hand remained outside the earth.
summary.zh: 香戈在奧沃為王，奧巴塔拉賜他一枚可勝萬敵的符咒；他吞下大半，餘者交妻歐雅保管——歐雅趁他不在也吃了。翌日朝會，輪到香戈啟口，他已形貌大變，口中噴火，滿朝盡散；歐雅與侍女亦然。香戈自知已成神，頓足於地，大地裂開，接他與三位妻子入地而去——只有他手中鐵鏈的一端留在了地面上。

sensitivity.note: Nagô legend recorded by Nina Rodrigues from Bahian tellers; variant of the Yoruba Shangó cycle. Cross-ref: yoruba Shango records.

passages.text: Changó would be, instead of being born of Yemanjá as in the preceding myth, a son of Obatalá, and began by reigning in Ovó, capital of Yoruba. One day Obatalá gave him a powerful charm which, when swallowed, made him capable of conquering all his enemies. Changó ate the greater part of the charm and gave the remainder to his wife Oyá to guard — who, in the absence of her husband, ate it too.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues, Os Africanos no Brasil (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: When the next day, in the council of the ministers, Changó's turn came to speak, he was transfigured, and flames came out of his mouth, which dispersed the whole audience; the same happened to Oyá with her ladies. Certain that he was now an orishá, Changó beat with his foot on the ground, which opened and gave him passage with his three wives. But there remained outside the earth the extremity of an iron chain that he carried in his hand.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Shangó under the Earth: the End of the Iron Chain

texts.period: Afro-Brazilian Nagô mythology; recorded late 19th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (1906), ch. on the Nagô religion — the variants of the death of Changó (Oyá's flight; the fisher Huisi; the hanged king and the chain)

summary.en: The variants of Changó's end chase one another: Oyá steals the charm, flees to her brother Olokun the sea, then to Olochá the lake, then hides with the fisher Huisi — who eats the stolen charm, becomes an orishá, and duels Changó with an uprooted tree against a canoe until the earth opens for the tired thunderer. In the euhemerized telling the missionaries circulate, Changó was the first king of Yoruba, deposed by the parrot-eggs and the message 'it is time to go sleep', who fled to the forests and hanged himself — and the mourners, going to find the corpse, found only a depression in the soil with the end of an iron chain: they nailed it to the ground, heard Changó speaking under the earth, built a little temple there, and knew that the king had not died but had turned orishá.
summary.zh: 香戈的結局諸版本互相追逐：歐雅竊符，先逃海兄奧洛昆、再逃湖姊奧洛夏，最後藏身漁夫懷西家中——懷西吞符成神，拔樹為兵與持舟作械的香戈決戰，力竭的雷神踏地遁走。教士們流傳的『人化神』版：香戈是約魯巴開國之王，因鸚鵡蛋之諭被廢，夜遁森林自縊；弔唁者尋屍不見，只見土窪中鐵鏈一端——釘鏈於地，聞地下有人言語，遂建小廟：王未死，已化為神。

sensitivity.note: Nagô variants recorded by Nina Rodrigues; the 'English missionary' euhemerization is attributed by the Bahian elders themselves to Protestant mission influence — preserved here as an internal debate about the god's historicity. Cross-ref: yoruba Shango records.

passages.text: A simple variant of the myth is that in which Oyá steals from her husband the remedy-charm. Terrified by the threats of Changó, Oyá went to take refuge in the palace of her brother Olokun, the sea. Accompanying unseen the sun that was setting, Changó went there; a violent fight was waged between Changó and Olokun, and in the meantime Oyá fled to the house of her sister Olochá, the lake. Changó pursued her, demolishing everything in his march, tearing up the trees by the roots and hurling them to great distances. Recognizing that her sister could not protect her, Oyá fled again and hid herself in the house of the fisher Huisi.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Terrified, the fisher asked Oyá how he, a simple mortal, could fight with an orishá like Changó; Oyá made him eat of the stolen charm, and Huisi, transformed into an orishá, went out to meet Changó, brandishing a tree he had torn up by the roots — there was no other in the place. Changó brandished as weapon the canoe of Huisi and charged his adversary. The arms broke at the first encounter, and the orishás fought body to body; unable to conquer, and fearful of being conquered, Changó, who began to feel himself fatigued, beat with his foot on the ground, which opened and received him. During the fight Oyá fled to Lokoró, where the people erected a temple to her.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Another version, found in Bahía principally among the negroes who were under the direction of the English missionaries in Lagos, gives to Changó an entirely euhemeristic origin — which our negroes generally attribute to the protestant missionaries, interested in robbing Changó of his qualities of orishá. Changó had been the first king of Yoruba. Tyrant and cruel, the people did not wish to suffer him any more, and, according to the custom of the country, sent him the bowl with the eggs of the parrot and the traditional message: 'that he must already be too much fatigued with the labors of government, and it was time to go and sleep' — which meant the king's retiring to his apartments and letting himself be strangled by his wives. But Changó did not conform to the intimación and resisted; he was defeated and sought to flee to Tapa, the land of his mother. He abandoned the palace at night, followed only by a slave and one of his women, and entered the forests; the woman abandoned him too. Lost in the forest he wandered for days without eating; at last he ordered the slave to await him in a given place until he returned — and the slave, tired of waiting, went to look for him and found him a few steps off, hanged on a tree.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: By chance the slave could discover the way and carried the news to Oyá. Fearful of being held responsible for the death of Changó, the magnates went at once to seek the cadaver — but they no longer found it. Near the tree there was a depression in the soil from which came the extremity of an iron chain. They nailed the end to the ground and heard Changó speaking under the earth. Thus they convinced themselves that Changó had not died, but had transformed himself into an orishá; there they constructed a small temple, and around it, more...
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: Odudua and the Hunter of Ado

region.en: Bahía, Brazil (Nagô tellings of the Ado legend)
region.zh: 巴西巴伊亞（納戈講述的阿多傳說）

texts.period: Afro-Brazilian Nagô mythology; recorded late 19th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (1906), ch. on the Nagô religion — Odudua and the great temple of Ado

summary.en: Thus must be understood some legends that celebrate the amorous adventures of Odudua, who from that time forward is Venus: the great temple of Odudua in Adó, fifteen miles north of Badagry, had this origin. In one of her hunting excursions through the forests, Odudua met one day a young hunter of such rare beauty that there instantly sprang up a violent passion in the ardent temperament of the orishá. They abandoned themselves easily in the same place to the satisfaction of that passion, and for some weeks enjoyed their delights in a hut the two had built. Sated at last, Odudua departed — but in grateful memory of that love so intense and so fleeting, she promised to constitute herself protectress of the mortals who should come to the place; and thither flowed at once all who sought divine protection there, and from the case the city took the name of Adó, which means lascivious man or woman.
summary.zh: 自此被視作維納斯的奧杜杜瓦，其情史傳說正解釋了阿多大廟之由來。一日林中狩獵，女神遇見俊美無雙的年輕獵人，熱烈的神性頓起狂愛；二人於原地搭棚相守數週。盡興之後奧杜杜瓦離去——然為記那濃烈卻短暫之愛，她允諾庇佑凡來此地之人；求神庇護者雲集，城因之得名『阿多』——意即放浪的男人或女人。

sensitivity.note: Nagô legend recorded by Nina Rodrigues (following Ellis's Yoruba material) from Bahian tradition. Cross-ref: yoruba Oduduwa records.

passages.text: Thus must be understood some legends in which are celebrated the amorous adventures of Odudua — for from here forward Odudua will be Venus. The great temple of Odudua in Adó, fifteen miles north of Badagry, had this origin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues, Os Africanos no Brasil (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: In one of her hunting excursions through the forests, Odudua met one day a young hunter of such rare beauty that there instantly sprang up a violent passion in the ardent temperament of the orishá. They abandoned themselves easily in the same place to the satisfaction of that passion of the moment, and for some weeks enjoyed their delights in a hut which the two had built.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: Sated at last, Odudua departed; but in grateful memory of that love so intense and so fleeting, she promised to constitute herself protectress of the mortals who should go there. There flowed at once all who sought in the place the divine protection, and from the case the city took the name of Adó, which means lascivious man or woman.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906), citing Ellis; not verbatim.

title.en: The Washing of the Bonfim: Senhor do Bonfim Is Obatalá
title.zh: 邦芬洗堂禮：邦芬主即奧巴塔拉

texts.period: Afro-Bahian religious practice; recorded late 19th c.; published 2024 (published 2026)

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (1906), ch. on survivals — the washing of the church of the Bomfim

summary.en: A Yoruba or Nagô religious practice still alive in Brazil: the washing of the church of the Bomfim is, for the Africans, creole and mixed-blood followers of the sect, a living cult — for Senhor do Bomfim, the Lord of the Good End, is Obatalá himself. Nina Rodrigues sets it against the carnival clubs of Rio — survivals by tradition rather than belief — and against the Afro-Bahian carnival clubs in which both currents flow at once: the Embaixada Africana celebrating a remembered Africa of kings and courts, the Pandegos da Africa parading the enthralled Africa itself down the city streets.
summary.zh: 一項在巴西仍鮮活的約魯巴宗教實踐：邦芬洗堂禮——對非洲裔、克里奧爾與混血的教眾而言，這是活的祭拜，因為『善終之主』邦芬主，正是奧巴塔拉本人。羅德里格斯將它與里約的狂歡節會（僅存於傳統記憶）相對照，又與巴伊亞的非裔狂歡會並列——那裡兩種血脈同時奔流：非洲大使會追憶國王與宮廷，『非洲樂事會』則把被奴役的非洲本身抬上街頭。

sensitivity.note: Description of a living syncretic feast (Lavagem do Bonfim) from Nina Rodrigues's typology of survivals; cross-ref: yoruba Obatala records.

passages.text: The distinction Nina Rodrigues establishes is between manifestations of a belief, a practice, a custom or feast African, still alive among us, and the tradition or recollection of sentiments that only existed in activity among our seniors. The washing of the church of the Bomfim is, as he demonstrated, a Yoruba or Nagô religious practice — but it is a truly living cult, for, for the Africans, creole negroes and mixed-bloods of that sect, the Senhor do Bomfim is Obatalá himself.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues, Os Africanos no Brasil (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: On the contrary, the carnival clubs of the Cucumby, of Rio de Janeiro, described by Dr. Mello Moraes, are popular feasts that have passed entirely to the state of tradition: the choice and the preference of the theme still betray the Black Race, but other races can associate themselves with those feasts, seeing in it only the element of characterization which is the essence of Carnival.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: There are finally intermediate or transitional cases, in which the African usage participates at the same time in tradition and in an institution still alive among us — the case of the African carnival clubs of Bahia, where of late the Bahian carnival is reduced almost to African clubs organized by some Africans, creole negroes and mixed-bloods. In the constitution of these clubs the two distinct sentiments reveal themselves: in some, like the Embaixada Africana, the dominant idea of the most intelligent or better-adapted negroes is the celebration of a survival, of a tradition — the characters and the motif taken from the cultivated peoples of Africa, Egyptians, Abyssinians. In the others there is, on the part of the directors, sometimes the intention of reviving traditions; but their popular success consists in their being true African popular feasts: the theme is uncultivated Africa that came enslaved to Brazil.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

title.en: The Pandegos da Africa: King Labossi in His Shell
title.zh: 非洲樂事會：貝殼中的拉博西王

region.zh: 巴西巴伊亞狂歡節街頭

source.work: Raimundo Nina Rodrigues, 'Os Africanos no Brasil' (1906), ch. on survivals — the Pandegos da Africa and the char of the Zambeze (Diario da Bahia, 16 Feb. 1899)

summary.en: The carnival car of the Pandegos da Africa 'represents the margin of the Zambeze, on whose bank, reclining in an immense shell, rests King Labossi, surrounded by his ministers Aua, Oman, Abato, the last bearing the standard of the club'; behind came a car with two members representing powerful personages of the king's court — Barborim, Roda; three cavaliers preceded the African charanga that came on foot, with their strident and impossible instruments. Then a car representing the hut of Pai Agen and his woman with the fetish-calabash, giving good luck to everything and everybody. A compact multitude of negroes and mixed-bloods, incorporated into it and accompanying it, singing the African songs, beating out their dances, hailing their idols or saints shown in the car of the fetish — one would say a colossal candomblé parading through the streets of the city; and in fact the felichist negroes thus avenged themselves of the intermittent impertinences of the police, exhibiting their feast in public.
summary.zh: 『非洲樂事會』的花車『再現贊比西河畔：拉博西王斜倚巨貝，由大臣阿瓦、奧曼、阿巴托環侍，末者高舉會旗』；後隨宮廷權貴之車，三位騎士先行，非洲樂班徒步相隨，奏著刺耳難名之樂；最後一車再現巫師阿真夫婦的茅屋與法力葫蘆——為萬物萬人賜福。黑奴與混血人群密匝匝地加入隊伍，唱非洲之歌、踏非洲之舞、向車中神偶歡呼——簡直是一場穿行街市的巨型康東布莱；巫俗信眾藉此向警察的刁難報復，把節慶公然抬上街頭。

sensitivity.note: Carnival-club description from contemporary Bahian press (Diario da Bahia, 1899) compiled by Nina Rodrigues; cross-ref: afroatlantic-bomfim-washing.

passages.text: In the Pandegos da Africa, the car, one diary describes, 'represents the margin of the Zambeze, on whose bank, reclining in an immense shell, rests the king Labossi, surrounded by his ministers Aua, Oman, Abato, the last bearing the standard of the club.' Behind came 'a car with two members representing powerful and influential personages of the court of the king — Barborim, Roda.' Three cavaliers preceded the African charanga that came on foot, with their strident and impossible instruments.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906), quoting a Bahian diary; not verbatim.

passages.text: Then, 'a car representing the hut of pai Agen and his woman with the caboré of fetish, to give good luck to everything and to everybody.' The success of this club was enormous: there was seen a compact multitude of negroes and mixed-bloods that had, so to speak, incorporated themselves into it and accompanied it singing the African songs, beating out their dances, and hailing the idols or saints that were shown to them in the car of the fetish. One would say a colossal candomblé parading through the streets of the city — and in fact the felichist negroes avenged themselves in this way of the intermittent impertinences of the police, exhibiting their feast in public.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.

passages.text: And it is not a small revenge after all — for, well counted, including all the bands that announce how many feasts of the outskirts exist, more than a dozen of these opportunities are organized annually. If this testimony of an eye-witness could be charged with partiality, it would be ratified by the unanimous transcription of the local press.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Nina Rodrigues (1906); not verbatim.
